titulo: Countable and uncountable / Determiners: some, any, a lot of
titulo_es: Countable and uncountable nouns (some, any, a lot of)
descripcion_es: Tell countable and uncountable nouns apart and use some, any and a lot of.
resumen: Countable nouns can be counted and have a plural (an apple, two apples); uncountable nouns have no plural and don't take a/an (water, money, information). Some, any and a lot of are used with both.

filas: water, rice, bread, money, music, advice
I've got some friends in Rome. Would you like some tea?
We haven't got any milk. Are there any questions?
a lot of cars, a lot of traffic

items: Some nouns are uncountable in English but countable in Spanish: advice (es: consejos), information (es: información), news (es: noticias), furniture (es: muebles), homework (es: deberes).
To count uncountable nouns, use units: a piece of advice, a glass of water, a loaf of bread, a bottle of wine.
News is uncountable and takes a singular verb: The news is good.

ejemplos.frase: There's some cheese in the fridge.
Can you give me some advice?
She drinks a lot of water.
I need some information about the course.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: She gave me a good advice.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: She gave me some good advice.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Advice is uncountable (also: a good piece of advice).
News is uncountable and takes a singular verb.

ejercicios.frase: Have you got ___ brothers or sisters?
ejercicios.explicacion: The second table on the card applies: any is used in negative sentences and questions. The clue is that the sentence is a question (Have you got…?) with countable nouns in the plural. That is why it is any; in Spanish it is not even translated.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Some is used in affirmative sentences and offers; in a neutral question, use any.
A goes with a singular countable noun; brothers and sisters are plural.

ejercicios.explicacion: The table says that some is used in affirmative sentences and offers; polite requests such as I'd like… work the same way. The clue is I'd like… please, an affirmative request. Water is uncountable, so it cannot take a, and some means “a little”.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Any is for negative sentences and questions; in an affirmative request, use some.
Water is uncountable and does not take a.

ejercicios.explicacion: This is the rule for any in negative sentences, from the second table. The clue is isn't, which makes the sentence negative. Rice is uncountable (it goes with is, not with are), and any is used with both uncountable nouns and plural countable nouns.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Some is for affirmative sentences; with the negative isn't you need any.
No is already negative; with isn't it would make a double negative. You would say There's no rice or There isn't any rice.

glosario.definicion_l: being or located on or directed toward the side of the body to the west when facing north · not used up

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with a, an or some.
ejercicios.explicacion: The first table says that countable nouns take a or an in the singular. Orange, the fruit, is countable, and because it starts with a vowel sound it takes an, not a. Some does not fit because some goes with plurals or uncountable nouns, and here it is about one orange.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Orange (the fruit) is countable and starts with a vowel.
ejercicios.traduccion: Me tomé una naranja para desayunar.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Orange starts with a vowel sound, so the article is an.
Some is not used with a singular countable noun; for one orange, use an.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with a, an or some.
ejercicios.explicacion: Bread is uncountable according to the first table, so it cannot take a or an. The clue is the noun bread and the fact that the sentence is a request (Can I have…, please?), where some is used. If you want to count bread, you have to use a unit: a loaf of bread.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Bread is uncountable: it cannot take a.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Bread is uncountable: it does not take a (a word-for-word copy of Spanish “un pan”).
Although it is a question, it is a request, and in requests some is used.

ejercicios.frase: The furniture in this room ___ very old.
ejercicios.explicacion: The list on the card says that furniture is uncountable in English, although Spanish says “los muebles” in the plural. The first table shows that uncountable nouns take a singular verb. That is why it is is, even though the Spanish translation has “son”.
ejercicios.traduccion: Los muebles de esta habitación son muy viejos.

errores_previstos.explicacion: A word-for-word copy of Spanish “los muebles son”: furniture is uncountable and takes a singular verb.

glosario.definicion_l: furnishings that make a room or other area ready for occupancy

ejercicios.explicacion: This is the rule for any in negative sentences. The clue is don't have, which makes the sentence negative, and money, which is uncountable. That is why it is any; a is not possible because money is not counted with the indefinite article.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Negative with an uncountable noun: any.

por_opcion.some: Incorrect: some is for affirmative sentences; in a negative sentence, use any.
por_opcion.any: Correct: a negative sentence with an uncountable noun.
por_opcion.a: Incorrect: money is uncountable and does not take a.

ejercicios.frase: There is a lot of ___ in the city centre.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table on the card gives a lot of traffic as an example of an uncountable noun. The clue is There is, in the singular, which needs an uncountable or singular noun after a lot of. Traffic is uncountable and has no plural. Cars would be correct with There are, but not with There is.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: There is goes with a singular or uncountable noun: traffic.
ejercicios.traduccion: Hay mucho tráfico en el centro de la ciudad.

por_opcion.traffic: Correct: uncountable, it agrees with There is.
por_opcion.traffics: Incorrect: traffic is uncountable and has no plural.
por_opcion.cars: Incorrect here: cars is plural and would need There are a lot of cars.

glosario.definicion_l: the aggregation of things (pedestrians or vehicles) coming and going in a particular locality during a specified period of time · buying and selling; especially illicit trade
the central part of a city

ejercicios.frase: Let me give you a piece of ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: The list on the card says that advice is uncountable and that, to count it, you use a piece of advice. The clue is a piece of, the unit that lets you count an uncountable noun. Advice has no plural, and advise (with s) is the verb (to give advice).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The uncountable noun is advice; advise is the verb.

por_opcion.advices: Incorrect: advice is uncountable and has no plural.
por_opcion.advice: Correct: an uncountable noun, counted with a piece of.
por_opcion.advise: Incorrect: it is the verb (to give advice); after a piece of you need the noun.

ejercicios.frase: The children have got a lot of ___ tonight.
ejercicios.explicacion: The list on the card includes homework (es: deberes) among the nouns that are uncountable in English but plural in Spanish. The clue is a lot of, which is used with both types, and the fact that homework takes neither a plural nor a. That is why the form is just homework.
ejercicios.traduccion: Los niños tienen muchos deberes esta noche.

por_opcion.homeworks: Incorrect: homework is uncountable and has no plural.
por_opcion.homework: Correct: uncountable, after a lot of.
por_opcion.a homework: Incorrect: an uncountable noun does not take a, and a lot of a is not possible anyway.

glosario.definicion_l: work, such as schoolwork or piecework, that is done at home

ejercicios.frase: I need some informations about trains.
respuestas: I need some information about trains.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is one of the typical mistakes on the card: information is uncountable and has no plural. The clue is the -s in informations, copied from Spanish “informaciones”. Just remove it; some is correct because the sentence is affirmative.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I need some informations about trains.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This leaves the sentence uncorrected: information has no plural.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I need an information about trains.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Information is uncountable and does not take an; for one item, say a piece of information.

glosario.definicion_l: a message received and understood · knowledge acquired through study or experience or instruction

ejercicios.frase: Would you like a milk in your tea?
respuestas: Would you like some milk in your tea?
Would you like milk in your tea?
ejercicios.explicacion: Milk is uncountable, so it does not take a. The clue is that Would you like…? is an offer, and for offers the card gives some. You can also leave out the determiner: Would you like milk in your tea?
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Milk is uncountable: it does not take a.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Would you like a milk in your tea?
errores_previstos.explicacion: This leaves the sentence uncorrected: milk is uncountable.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Would you like some milks in your tea?
errores_previstos.explicacion: Milk is uncountable and has no plural: some milk.

ejercicios.frase: The news are on at nine.
respuestas: The news is on at nine.
ejercicios.explicacion: The list on the card points out that news is uncountable and takes a singular verb, even though it ends in -s. The clue is are, copied from Spanish “las noticias son”. You need is. Here, be on means that the programme is being broadcast.
ejercicios.traduccion: Las noticias son a las nueve.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The news are on at nine.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This leaves the sentence uncorrected: news takes a singular verb.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The new is on at nine.
errores_previstos.explicacion: News is not the plural of new: it is an uncountable word that always ends in -s.

glosario.definicion_l: appear in a show, on T.V. or radio

ejercicios.explicacion: It is a negative sentence with any, as the second table shows. The order is subject (We) + haven't got + any + plural noun (eggs). Eggs is countable, and in negative sentences any goes with plurals just as it does with uncountable nouns.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Got is part of the verb have got and goes right after haven't: haven't got any.
That is question word order; the sentence required is negative.

respuestas: He drinks a lot of coffee
ejercicios.explicacion: The second table says that a lot of is used with countable and uncountable nouns. Coffee is uncountable, and the structure is subject (He) + verb (drinks) + a lot of + noun. A lot of is a fixed three-word expression that always goes in that order.

errores_previstos.respuesta: He drinks lot a of coffee
errores_previstos.explicacion: The fixed expression is a lot of, with a at the start.

errores_previstos.respuesta: He drinks coffee a lot of
errores_previstos.explicacion: A lot of goes before the noun, not after it.

descripcion_larga_es: Countable nouns can be counted and have a plural (an apple, two apples); uncountable nouns have no plural and don't take a or an (water, money, information). This difference decides the article, the verb and words such as some, any or a lot of. Spanish speakers find it difficult because several words that are countable in Spanish (consejo, información, mueble, noticia, deberes) are uncountable in English.

contexto.que_es: It is the grammatical difference between nouns that are counted as units (book, egg, person) and nouns for substances, materials or ideas (water, rice, music, advice). Countable nouns can take a, an and a plural; uncountable nouns cannot, and they take a singular verb. Some is used in affirmative sentences and offers, any in negative sentences and questions, and a lot of with both.
contexto.por_que_importa: Mistakes such as an advice, informations or the news are are among the most common for Spanish speakers and appear in any exam marking. The difference also affects other structures: much or many, few or little, a singular or plural verb. Mastering it from A1 level prevents mistakes that later become fixed habits.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: Every time you talk about quantities: shopping, food, money, advice, furniture or the news. The signal is the noun itself: if it names a substance or something abstract, it is probably uncountable. Where Spanish says “un consejo” or “unas informaciones”, English says a piece of advice or some information.
